papers.title: Who Takes the Lead? Model Ability and Task-Conditioned Collaboration with Humans
papers.abstract: As language-model agents grow more capable, they can carry more of a task without asking anyone for help. Falling reliance on a human partner is easy to read as a failure of collaboration when it may instead be a correct division of labor, and the rate of human involvement alone cannot tell the two apart. We study this systematically by placing an agent and a person under a shared objective while varying who holds the advantage: the human has a clear advantage, neither does, or the agent does. To obtain this control, we introduce a shared-control maze, in which an agent-controlled and a human-controlled avatar share the objective of reaching a common target in as few team turns as possible. The agent allocates each team turn between acting itself and handing the move to the person, and initial placement sets the human's shortest-path advantage while the task is otherwise unchanged. We evaluate GPT~5.6~Sol, Command~A+, Qwen~3.8~27B, and Command~R, first measuring solo capability with a single avatar and full-map observability, then running co-play with human participants across the three advantage conditions. Across the four models, stronger solo performance is associated with selective, route-conditioned human involvement: the models that solve the maze reliably on their own act for themselves almost without exception when the human holds no advantage, and involve the human on roughly $80\%$ of initial decisions when the human route is shorter. Command R, the model with substantially weaker solo performance, shows no such selectivity.

papers.title: Too Long to Watch, Too Short to Leave: Designing for Agent Micro-Waits
papers.abstract: Agentic systems increasingly carry out complex work, where a single turn routinely runs for minutes. This produces a micro-wait that is too long to watch and too short to leave. In a formative study with 12 daily agent users, we found that staying felt like wasted time, while switching away fragmented attention and forfeited the context needed to re-engage. We introduce Sidecar, a parallel assistant situated in the same interface as the agent, which reads the run and surfaces implicit decisions the agent made, along with task directions worth exploring. In a within-subjects study (N=16), Sidecar helped participants stay focused on their main task, freely workshop unfinished ideas without fear of unwanted action, and recognize under-specification in their own prompts. Together, these findings contribute to designs that help users stay context-aware and engaged during agent micro-waits.

papers.title: CanvasObs: Structured Spatial Observation for Agent Editing on 2D Infinite Canvases
papers.abstract: Editing agents on 2D infinite canvases must reason about application state that pixels may not reveal. Targets may be offscreen or covered, while visual containment and touching arrows may disagree with recorded frame membership or connector bindings. We ask how a structured observation layer can support accurate object selection during agentic editing on 2D infinite canvases. We present CanvasObs, which augments visual context with a structured payload and guidance for reading four components: Identity & State, Visibility & Structure, Relations, and Offscreen Object bounds in action coordinates. A Remote Team Handoff case study illustrates retrieving an editable offscreen copy, choosing a covered chart by color, separating cards by frame membership, and preserving an evidence connection. We turn these cases into ten controlled configurations and compare CanvasObs with the baseline agent in 1,200 browser trials across three models. CanvasObs improves Correct target for every model. Combined across models, it raises Correct target from 16.5% to 48.3%, an increase of 31.8 percentage points (95% confidence interval [29.0, 34.7]), and Full task success from 4.3% to 25.0%. These results show that compact structured observation can improve object choice on 2D infinite canvases without redesigning the editing pipeline.

papers.title: "It Wouldn't Have Been So Apparent to Me": Evaluating How Thought-Level Progress Tracking Supports Psychosocial Goals
papers.abstract: We pursue psychosocial goals every day, from coping with anxiety, to pursuing personal growth. While prior research has designed systems for tracking progress towards behavioral goals, fewer studies have focused on progress towards psychosocial goals - and the thinking changes people make to address them. As a first step, we present Thought-GPS, a system that visualizes potential markers of such thought-level progress in-the-moment as users interact with an AI-supported cognitive restructuring intervention. We evaluated Thought-GPS through a mixed-methods single-session study with 30 participants, comparing Thought-GPS with an active control condition without progress markers. We found preliminary evidence that participants using Thought-GPS reported greater clarity about how they might change to pursue their goals, stronger motivation to reflect on goal progress, and greater engagement in that reflection. Participants also reported that progress markers made subtle progress visible, helped them engage in deeper reflection, and connect conversational insights to their personal goals.

papers.title: ValiAssist: Scaling LLM-generated Programming Feedback Validation by Demonstration
papers.abstract: Generative AI can create programming feedback at scale, but validating its alignment with instructors' pedagogical goals and strategies remains challenging. Instructors may struggle to fully specify validation criteria upfront, as these often emerge through inspecting concrete examples and revising misaligned feedback. We present ValiAssist, a validation-by-demonstration system that infers reusable validation logic from instructors' revisions of AI-generated feedback and allows instructors to inspect and refine that logic as it is applied across other student submissions. In a comparative study with 16 instructors, ValiAssist helped instructors create and refine validation criteria, producing feedback that better aligned with their pedagogical intent (91% vs. 57%) and more than doubling the accuracy of correcting problematic criteria (77% vs. 32%). Our findings suggest that validation by demonstration can help instructors turn judgments they know how to make on individual cases into explicit, reusable logic, while progressively clarifying where those judgments do and do not generalize.

papers.title: The Differential Effects of AI Abstention on Advice Acceptance
papers.abstract: AI advising systems are typically designed to always provide a response. Recent work has focused on developing systems that withhold advice in some instances, such as when advice quality is questionable, to improve the overall quality of guidance when it is given; a design paradigm we refer to as AI abstention. While substantial work has focused on optimizing when models should abstain, little is known about how users respond to systems that abstain. In a preregistered experiment, participants made repeated financial decisions, assisted by one of two advising regimes: an AI that advises selectively or one that advises on every decision. We find that the same AI abstention regime produces differential effects depending on the user: it increases advice acceptance among users with high perceived expertise and tends to decrease it among users with low perceived expertise. This differential effect is accounted for by the cognitive burden users face when repeatedly reconciling AI recommendations with their own judgment; AI abstention appears to relieve this burden among users with high perceived expertise, and in doing so increases their receptivity to advice. Further, AI abstention mitigates the decline in advice acceptance observed among expert users over repeated interactions. Exploratory evidence also suggests it increases appropriate acceptance where advice would improve the decision, increasing the downstream accuracy of perceived experts. The AI abstention regime is thus a first-order design property of AI advisory systems, and one that must be calibrated to the users a system serves.

papers.title: Inspectable LLM-Simulated Participants for Qualitative Interview Rehearsal
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used across research workflows, including research ideation, qualitative analysis, and participant simulation. Within work on participant simulation, prior studies have largely evaluated simulated participants by how realistic or human-like their responses appear, leaving less known about how researchers use and critique these materials when revising interview protocols before fieldwork. We present Rehearsim, an inspectable research probe that treats LLM-simulated participants as materials for methodological rehearsal rather than substitutes for human participants. Rehearsim combines literature-grounded participant construction, interactive interview rehearsal, and traceable thematic review while keeping protocol decisions under researcher control. In a study with 21 qualitative researchers, participants used simulated materials to surface assumptions and gaps, reconsider participant populations, revise target populations, and develop follow-up probes. They also identified risks, including the concealment of weak questions, dismissal of unexpected synthetic details, and interpretive anchoring from generated themes. We derive an inspectable-rehearsal framework emphasizing traceability, contestability, researcher control, and epistemic boundaries.

papers.title: Relational Complexity: Making Sense of Social Companion AI Use
papers.abstract: The adoption of social companion AI (SCAI) is often framed in terms of the positive features it offers users, including its nonjudgemental nature, agreeableness, and availability. Here, we argue the appeal of these features primarily arises from the difficulties inherent in human sociality. SCAI reduces what we term relational complexity, or the demands and risks inherent in human relationships. Drawing insights from studies of human cognition, communication, and human-computer interaction, we identify six distinct sites of relational complexity that we posit are integral to understanding SCAI adoption. These include: (i) relationship formation and dissolution; (ii) achieving mutual understanding; (iii) interpersonal motives and strategic uncertainty; (iv) social partner evaluation and self-presentation; (v) social embeddedness and information flow; and (vi) reciprocity and relationship maintenance. By attenuating relational complexity, SCAI offers users some of the experiences associated with companionship while reducing the demands intrinsic to obtaining such experiences from another person. However, the lower interpersonal risk and diminished cognitive load that attracts users to SCAI may contribute to myriad negative impacts, including relationship displacement, social demotivation, social deskilling, and risks to privacy. The concept of relational complexity thus provides a framework for studying both the appeal of artificial companionship and its implications for human wellbeing.

papers.title: Bias and Reliability in Learning-Style Inference from Student--AI Dialogues: An Evaluation of GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational technologies for personalized support, creating opportunities for real-time learner modeling from dialogue. This study evaluates whether GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash can infer three Felder-Silverman Learning Style Model dimensions (Active-Reflective, Sensing-Intuitive, and Sequential-Global) from short, task-focused student-AI problem-solving dialogues. Using questionnaire-derived Index of Learning Styles labels from 153 undergraduate participants, we compared deterministic zero-shot and few-shot prompting under five-fold cross-validation. Although accuracy and support-weighted F1 were moderate for Sensing-Intuitive and Sequential-Global, majority-class baselines, macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and per-class recall showed that performance was often driven by dominant-label prediction rather than reliable recognition of both classes. The models substantially under-identified Intuitive and Global learners; few-shot prompting produced mixed effects and sometimes amplified majority-class bias. Active-Reflective classification remained unstable across models. These findings indicate that LLM-generated learner-style labels should be treated as uncertain, bias-prone signals rather than stable learner profiles, and that dialogue-based personalization systems require bias-aware evaluation and uncertainty-sensitive design.

papers.title: What should AI forget? A design and taxonomy for negative space governance in AI memory
papers.abstract: AI memory personalizes assistants, yet users want some disclosed information forgotten. We characterize the negative space of AI memory, where protection should take precedence over potential future personalization benefits. From 179 incidents reported by 146 users, we developed a taxonomy of 15 information categories users want excluded from memory, revealing sensitivity concerns beyond conventional taxonomies. We operationalize this taxonomy in FENCE, a policy-level memory gate that automatically applies user-selected category-based rules to subsequent conversations, preventing information from protected conversations from entering AI memory by default while allowing case-by-case overrides. In a within-subjects study (N=15), participants described FENCE as making memory governance more usable, interpretable, and trustworthy than conventional post-hoc management. Our findings demonstrate how taxonomy-based rules can potentially support user-defined memory boundaries. We call for collective efforts to establish policies governing what AI should not remember, rather than leaving protection to individual retrospective management.

papers.title: CAESAR: Mixed Reality Search-and-Rescue Platform for Cognitive Attack Evaluation
papers.abstract: Mixed Reality (MR) enables immersive training by tightly coupling virtual content with the physical environment and supporting embodied interaction. In safety-critical collaborative tasks such as search-and-rescue, however, users rely heavily on virtual elements for perception, coordination, and decision-making, making them vulnerable to cognitive attacks that subtly distort visual feedback, virtual content, or system synchronization. While prior MR security research has examined individual attack mechanisms, evaluations are typically conducted in isolated or single-user settings, and there is a lack of standardized collaborative testbeds for systematic adversarial experimentation. In this paper, we develop CAESAR, an end-to-end multi-user MR framework for systematic evaluation of cognitive attacks in collaborative search-and-rescue training. CAESAR features a modular architecture that integrates four classes of cognitive attacks within a synchronized collaborative scenario and incorporates a multimodal data collection pipeline that captures behavioral, performance, and subjective measures under adversarial conditions. We conduct a controlled user study with an in-depth analysis of the latency-based attack, demonstrating measurable effects on task performance and user behavior while characterizing users' subjective experience under adversarial conditions.

papers.title: Looks Fine to Me: Understanding Oversight in Agentic Interactions
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though flawed outputs may appear convincing. Our formative study (N=12) revealed that users accepted plausible outputs without thorough evaluation, and only recognized these lapses in retrospect. To examine this systematically, we conducted a controlled within-subject study (N=36) in which participants completed programming tasks with an agent that produced correct outputs, silent defects, or visible failures. Combining task outcomes, interaction logs, gaze, physiological signals, and self-reports, we examined perceived, behavioral, and effective oversight. Participants were often highly confident while missing silent defects: they performed generic checks, failed to generate diagnostic evidence, or even misinterpreted defect evidence. We discuss how studying oversight across multiple dimensions can support future work on timely, task-calibrated re-engagement.

papers.title: Digital Nudge Effects in Optimal Stopping Games: Antagonistic Interactions in Layered Choice Architectures
papers.abstract: Digital nudges have become a prominent area of research in human-centered interaction, yet little is known about how they interact when deployed together. This study examines the individual and combined effects of anchoring, salience, and social proof digital nudges on stopping behavior and outcome quality in a sequential decision task. Using a 2^3 between-subjects factorial design grounded in the secretary problem (N = 181), we find that (1) an anchor nudge significantly increased exploration rather than constraining it (b = 1.207, p = .017); (2) the salience nudge produced the smallest effect of any condition; and (3) combining the anchor and social proof nudges produced the worst outcome quality of any condition ($181.83 vs. $192.21 for anchor-only), with outcome quality declining monotonically as nudge count increased. These findings provide the first controlled evidence for a digital nudge crowding-out effect with direct implications for the ethical design of digital interfaces.

papers.title: The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.

papers.title: The Labor of Storytelling: How People with Chronic Illnesses Leverage AI and Communities for Narrative Translation
papers.abstract: The distinctiveness of people with chronic illness as storytellers is how they experience their illness. Symptoms, pain, and biological disruptions are eloquent forms of speech of the body that beget social articulation. The stories people tell about illness shape how suffering is legitimized, and acted upon. Large language models have emerged as new mediators within this landscape---a role once predominantly supported by communities. In doing so, these systems participate in what we term narrative translation: transforming lived illness experiences for particular audiences and purposes. Through 21 prototype-driven semi-structured interviews with people with chronic illness, we contribute an empirical account of how participants navigate this mediation alongside existing sources of support. Our findings surface distinct yet complementary roles participants envisioned for AI and their communities, and how trust in AI was shaped by learning model-boundaries and perceiving understanding. We characterize these findings to inform future designs of AI-mediated narrative support.

papers.title: TracePrism: Extending Semantic Trace Topics to Iterative, Encoding-Aware Trace Partitioning
papers.abstract: Process mining typically explains an event log with a single model, clustering, or classifier fitted to all cases, although real logs often mix cases that follow different sub-processes. Trace clustering separates sub-populations, but it fixes one notion of trace similarity for the whole analysis. We propose TracePrism, which treats process discovery as iterative partitioning with three characteristics. The trace encoding is adaptive: it is chosen for each working set of remaining traces from a library of encodings, with suggestions scored for that set. The partitioning is iterative: the analyst forms a candidate group based on a rule, a dominant topic, a cluster over topic weights, or a region of an embedding, accepts it if it is coherent in both process structure and outcome, and continues with the remaining traces. Decisions are revisable and recorded: a group can be reopened under a different working set or encoding, and the findings repository keeps both the earlier decision and its revision. We implement TracePrism as an open-source prototype and demonstrate it in usage scenarios on three real-world event logs. The scenarios also revealed behavior that we had not anticipated, such as process drift.

papers.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

papers.title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .

papers.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring behavioral vulnerability, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

papers.title: PhonoBridge: Error-Aware Phoneme-Mediated EMG-to-Text Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Electromyography (EMG) provides a non-invasive means of decoding silently articulated speech into text, but accurate decoding remains challenging due to limited availability of paired EMG-text data. We introduce PhonoBridge, a two-stage framework comprising a channel-aware EMG-to-phoneme frontend and a large language model (LLM) backend for text reconstruction. The frontend is trained on paired EMG-text data that consists of channel-wise feature extraction, cross-channel fusion, and electrode embeddings. With phonemes as the intermediate representation, we expand the backend's training data by converting LibriSpeech transcripts into phoneme-text pairs without additional EMG recordings. To adapt the LLM to frontend noise, we introduce Error-Profile-Guided Augmentation (EPGA), which perturbs transcript-derived phoneme sequences according to error patterns estimated from frontend predictions, generating additional training pairs for the LLM. On the Open Vocabulary silent-speech dataset, PhonoBridge achieves 24.77% WER, outperforming the previously reported best of 28.27% on the same test split.

papers.title: VISH-ASR: Viterbi-Guided Selection of Hotwords for Speech-LLM Contextual ASR
papers.abstract: Prompt-based contextual ASR requires selecting a compact hotword subset from large dynamic inventories, yet existing pre-selection methods rely either on discrete ASR hypotheses that may discard acoustic evidence or on separately trained retrieval models. We propose Viterbi-guided Selection of Hotwords (VISH), a training-free, plug-and-play framework that directly verifies candidate-specific acoustic support over frame-level CTC posteriors. VISH formulates pre-selection as constrained posterior search; M-VISH makes large-list verification scalable through frame-synchronous shared-prefix Viterbi search with bounded top-K pruning, while Bi-MVISH exploits complementary backward evidence for robust verification. Across five benchmarks, M-VISH achieves up to 11.7% absolute improvement in Best-F1 over a strong learned-retrieval baseline and reduces candidate-search latency by 75.2% at 2,000 candidates relative to hypothesis-based filtering. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of posterior-level verification for accurate and scalable hotword pre-selection without additional model training.

papers.title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
papers.abstract: Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter-trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined. We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe. In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized. The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape. We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints. Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds. Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds. The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together. A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them. Project page: https://omron-sinicx.github.io/point-hand/

papers.title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
papers.abstract: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different types of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

papers.title: Unpacking "Personal" Health Informatics for Proactive Collective Care
papers.abstract: Care is primarily a collective phenomenon, with a practice that involves sharing health and wellbeing information within a trusted "care circle" of family and companions for sensemaking, interpretation, decision-making, and follow-through. However, current digital health tools and systems are designed for individuals and primarily intended for Personal Health Informatics (PHI). This mismatch between collective practice and individualistic design creates new challenges for the proactive use of such systems in care settings and limits adoption, sustained engagement, and meaningful use. To examine how people practice collective care and how (if) they perceive, adopt, and integrate PHI systems for proactive care, we conducted a sequential mixed-methods study. Through an initial survey (n=87) and semi-structured interviews (n=22), we found that their practices involve collectively analyzing and sensemaking health information. However, we also found that their use of existing systems to support such practices is constrained by factors at personal, relational, technological, and structural levels that evolve over time. To address these constraints and explore redesigning PHI toward "Collective Health Informatics", we conducted eight stakeholder interviews (n=12), a follow-up survey (n=114), and six co-design workshops (n=12) to understand the dynamics required in collective settings while retaining agency. Using a design probe evaluation (n=38), we refine a design vision for coordinated, trustworthy action across such care relationships. Our findings motivate CC-Proact, an operational map that translates ecological influences into three design levers: Agency, Elicitation, and Engagement. Using this map, our work empirically examines collective care practices and offers six design recommendations to build responsible systems that proactively support collective care.

papers.title: An Interactive Framework for Personalised Urban Accessibility Assessment
papers.abstract: Publicly available walkability tools are easy to use but place-based: they assign the same value to everyone sharing a location, computed from fixed category weights and category definitions calibrated on North American service landscapes. Accessibility research has long held that accessibility varies among individuals at the same location, and has accordingly developed preference- and person-sensitive measures; those measures are run as analyst-operated geographic information system workflows, out of reach of the residents whose preferences they represent. We present a deployed framework in which the preference structure is supplied by the user at query time. A user states which amenity categories matter, how much each matters, which are non-negotiable, which to avoid, which substitute for one another, and how far they will walk for each, and the map updates accordingly. This is possible because a rectangular travel impedance reduces the measure to the number of amenities reachable within a user-set threshold, which can be precomputed via shortest-path routing, leaving only arithmetic at query time. The score also stays interpretable: it is bounded, and each category's contribution can be read on its own. We evaluate the framework across Bengaluru, reporting its sensitivity to discretisation choices and comparing it against existing measures using identical inputs. Configuration moves ward rankings considerably more than the choice of aggregation does.

papers.title: When Language Learners Code-Switch: Korean-English Code-Switching in LLM-based Speaking Practice
papers.abstract: Code-switching (CSW), the use of multiple languages within the same interaction, has been widely studied in NLP for multilingual communication. While CSW also occurs in language-learning contexts, the functions and pedagogical implications of learner CSW in learner-AI interactions remain underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce LAKE, a dataset of Learner-AI dialogues with Korean-English CSW. This dataset captures South Korean learners' CSW behavior during English speaking practice with LLM-based conversation partners, comprising 675 dialogues, 19.6K utterances, and 43.9 hours of learner speech. We develop a taxonomy of learner CSW functions, finding that learners switch to Korean for diverse purposes, including signaling lexical gaps, negotiating meaning, and conveying culturally specific content. We also observe learners reusing and adapting English expressions introduced by the LLM partner following their code-switches, suggesting opportunities for contextualized lexical support. To support research on speech recognition for learner CSW, we release 4.9 hours of code-switched learner speech with human-verified transcripts and benchmark speech-to-text models on Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), revealing difficulties in recognizing learner CSW. These findings highlight learner CSW as a communicative and pedagogically meaningful resource that can inform the design of AI-based conversational language learning systems.

papers.title: Evaluation format, not only model capability, shapes measured triage failure in consumer health AI
papers.abstract: A recent Nature Medicine study reported that ChatGPT Health under-triages 51.6% of emergencies and concluded that consumer-facing AI triage poses safety risks. Its protocol, however, was an exam-style scaffold (forced A/B/C/D output, knowledge suppression, no clarifying questions) unlike how consumers use health chatbots. We ask how much of the headline error rate is a property of the measurement rather than of the models. In a first, mechanistic study, five frontier LLMs on a 17-scenario bank scored 6.4 points higher under naturalistic patient-style messages than under the constrained scaffold (p=0.015). In a second, faithful replication we ran the authors' own 60 released vignettes through six frontier models under four matched formats, with clinician validation of the rewrites and a blinded clinician audit of the LLM adjudicators. Here the direction reversed: free-text rewrites scored slightly below the exact prompt (78.7% vs 81.8%, p=0.020), removing only the answer scaffold changed little (80.6% vs 81.4%, p=0.81), and naturalistic input with a forced categorical answer beat both the exact prompt (84.4%, p=0.023) and free text (p=0.0001). On the four vignettes defining the original emergency rate, under-triage was 17% with the exact scaffold, 50% in free text, and 21% with a forced letter on the same message; every free-text "under-triage" was a same-day recommendation scored C rather than D, and 60% made escalation conditional on information the patient was asked to check, behavior a single-turn benchmark cannot score. The headline rate did not reproduce as a stable cross-model finding; much of it depends on output format and on mapping prose onto a four-point scale. Each format elicits a separate response, so the design measures format sensitivity, not format versus capability. Safety claims should report sensitivity to input wording, output format and adjudication.

papers.title: Decision-Oriented Programming with Aporia
papers.abstract: AI agents help developers express computational intent abstractly, but at a cost: developers cede decision-making authority to agents, often without realizing that important design decisions are being made without them. We bring these decisions to the foreground in a workflow we dub decision-oriented programming. In DOP, decisions are (1) explicit and structured, serving as the shared medium between programmer and agent; (2) co-authored interactively, with the agent eliciting them from the programmer; and (3) traceable to code. As a step towards this vision, we built Aporia, a design probe that tracks decisions in a persistent, editable Decision Bank; elicits them proactively through design questions; and encodes each as a test suite that can help validate the agent's implementation. A study of 14 programmers showed that structuring collaboration around decisions kept programmer and agent in sync throughout the design process, and highlighted opportunities to better support programmer decision-making in future systems.

papers.title: WhatIf: Interactive Exploration of Large-Scale LLM Agent Simulations for Policy Reasoning
papers.abstract: Policymakers in domains such as emergency management, public health, and urban planning must make decisions under deep uncertainty, where outcomes depend on how large populations interpret information, coordinate, and adopt over time. Existing tools only partially support this process: tabletop exercises enable collaborative discussion but lack dynamic feedback, while computational simulations capture population dynamics but are designed for offline analysis. We present WhatIf, an interactive system that enables policymakers to steer, inspect, and compare LLM-powered social simulations in real time. Informed by a formative study in emergency preparedness planning, we derive four design requirements for interactive policy simulations: fluid steering, real-time scale, collaborative exploration, and multi-level interpretability. We developed WhatIf guided by these requirements and evaluated it with five preparedness professionals across three disaster evacuation scenarios. Our findings show that participants used the system as a space for iterative branching and comparison rather than evaluating fixed plans; reflected on tacit planning assumptions when agent behavior violated expectations; surfaced previously unrecognized planning vulnerabilities; and grounded their reasoning in inspectable agent-level cases rather than aggregate outputs alone. These findings suggest broader design implications for LLM-powered social simulation systems: designing such systems as interactive, shared reasoning environments--rather than offline predictive tools--can better support expert decision-making under deep uncertainty.

papers.title: Analyzing Human Heuristics and Strategies in Everyday Decision-Making Conversations for Conversational AI Design
papers.abstract: Conversational AI increasingly supports everyday decision-making, yet most systems rely on data-centric reasoning rather than the heuristic and interactional strategies people use in natural conversation. To ground design in actual human practice, we analyze 955 real-world Korean conversations (15,476 utterances) involving food and travel decisions, applying a decision-making codebook through an LLM-assisted coding pipeline. Our findings reveal that people prioritize satisficing over optimization, relying heavily on internal knowledge and interactional strategies to manage cognitive load. Critically, we identify a frequency-efficiency mismatch: the most prevalent heuristics sustain conversational flow during exploration, whereas infrequent, rule-based strategies are highly effective at driving resolution during exploitation. By mapping how these patterns transfer across the spectrum of human-AI interaction, this work provides empirical grounding consistent with cognitive theories of decision-making and offers design implications that align AI systems with human heuristic processes.

papers.title: Sketch Bug: Using Sketch-Based Input for Interactive Code Debugging
papers.abstract: We investigate sketch-like pen input as an alternative way to support execution control in interactive debugging. In our interface, programmers draw lightweight marks to set breakpoints, use symbolic strokes to control execution, and extend strokes into spirals to repeat traversal actions. The prototype combines gesture recognition with Python execution tracing in a conventional editor interface. In a controlled study with 24 programmers, we compared the sketch interface with conventional mouse-and-keyboard input on debugging tasks that required breakpoint placement, step-wise execution, and runtime state inspection. The results show that sketch-like input can support these execution-control tasks, while also introducing challenges in precision, recognition, and gesture recall. Our findings suggest that pen input is most promising where debugger interactions benefit from spatial grounding or continuous movement, rather than as a wholesale replacement for conventional debugging controls.

papers.title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
papers.abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, U.S. adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1042) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multi-turn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found some suggestive evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in some -- but not all -- analyses of different conspiratorial beliefs one to two months later. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, cognitively-focused interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

papers.title: Living with AI Companions: Sustained AI Companionship Predicts Lower Well-Being Through Lower Human Interaction
papers.abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly used for companionship, emotional support, and personal self-disclosure; however, how social engagement with these systems unfolds over time and shapes users' well-being remains unclear. To address this, we conducted a two-wave longitudinal study of CharacterAI users, surveying 1,182 participants at baseline and 439 after a mean follow-up of 12 months. We examined how social engagement with AI companions evolves and how these longitudinal engagement patterns may influence well-being through two hypothesized pathways: sustained social engagement over time and the displacement of human social interaction. We found that interaction intensity, companionship use, and self-disclosure all showed substantial continuity over time. Greater interaction intensity at baseline predicted greater subsequent interaction intensity, companionship use, and self-disclosure. Consistent with the longitudinal engagement pathway, sustained social engagement across these dimensions was consistently associated with lower well-being. Results further support the social displacement pathway, indicating that these links were mainly explained by lower in-person social interaction. These findings highlight the importance of designing AI companions that support human social relationships without displacing them.

papers.title: Flow Control: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models with Simple Real-Time Inputs
papers.abstract: We introduce flow control of vision-language-action (VLA) models, a simple and effective way to steer VLA actions in real time through generic inputs, such as a keyboard. This method can be used out-of-the-box and does not require retraining or fine-tuning VLAs. It enables relatively crude user inputs to steer a VLA to align with user intent. Flow control writes the user input into the initial condition of the VLA's flow matching action expert. Because the flow is deterministic, integration retains information about the user input while moving it toward the action distribution learned during training, so that the generated actions reflect the user's intent (high fidelity) and stay close to the VLA's own unsteered actions (high conformity). We demonstrate that flow control has many desirable properties: (1) flow control accurately and responsively steers robot actions with user inputs, (2) it is robust to suboptimal user inputs, (3) it enables users to steer VLAs to achieve significantly higher success rates and faster task completion, and (4) fine-tuning a VLA on flow control trajectories improves the autonomous policy. Together, these results provide a simple and intuitive way for users to help steer VLA actions, increasing task performance. Project page and videos: https://jcykao.github.io/flowcontrol/.

papers.title: Unified Agentic Video Editing Across Levels of Complexity and Creativity
papers.abstract: Editing is a core component of video production, requiring creative planning and decisions under multiple constraints. Here, we report methods for agentic tooling for automated video editing across three tasks varying in editorial goal, complexity and creativity, namely scene previews, video summaries and cinematic trailers. We evaluate the outputs and discuss implications for automation and agency.

papers.title: AI Misconception and Adoption Among Indonesian K-12 Teachers
papers.abstract: Indonesia's fragmented geography and uneven infrastructure pose persistent challenges for adopting new educational technologies. While national initiatives aim to mainstream AI in K-12 schools by 2025, policy readiness does not automatically mean teachers are ready for the classroom. This study surveys Indonesian K-12 teachers to examine: (1) their understanding of AI, (2) how they and their students use AI, and (3) their views on the acceptability of AI in learning activities. Through semi-automated thematic analysis, we identify common misconceptions and use cases. Our findings reveal a notable mismatch: while teachers find AI use in education acceptable and support it for the sake of efficiency, they remain fully aware of the risks to learning depth and academic honesty. We also find that this high level of acceptance is currently coupled with a poor understanding of how AI actually works.

papers.title: Comparing Computer Use Behavior Across Multiple Levels of Abstraction
papers.abstract: Interaction traces record how people and agents use computers, and comparing them can reveal usability barriers, differences in expertise, and human--agent similarity. Yet traces are recorded as low-level, interface-specific actions, making comparisons difficult across tasks, interfaces, and input modalities. Existing approaches either compare these actions directly, reduce traces to aggregate outcomes, or summarize them at higher-level goals, obscuring where behavior differs. We present MAP (Multi-level Action Parsing), a hierarchical semantic representation and annotation pipeline that maps traces into a common vocabulary across linked levels of abstraction. MAP compares traces by sequence, recurring patterns, and effort, localizing differences by type and abstraction level. A technical evaluation across three computer use datasets shows high agreement with manual annotations and broad coverage of behavior. Applying MAP shows that sighted and blind users increasingly converge at higher levels despite navigation differences, while agents omit corrective, help-seeking, and recovery behaviors present in human traces.

papers.title: TapID: Rapid touch interaction in virtual reality using wearable sensing
papers.abstract: Current Virtual Reality systems typically use cameras to capture user input from controllers or free-hand mid-air interaction. In this paper, we argue that this is a key impediment to productivity scenarios in VR, which require continued interaction over prolonged periods of time---a requirement that controller or free-hand input in mid-air does not satisfy. To address this challenge, we bring rapid touch interaction on surfaces to Virtual Reality---the input modality that users have grown used to on phones and tablets for continued use. We present TapID, a wrist-based inertial sensing system that complements headset-tracked hand poses to trigger input in VR. TapID embeds a pair of inertial sensors in a flexible strap, one at either side of the wrist; from the combination of registered signals, TapID reliably detects surface touch events and, more importantly, identifies the finger used for touch. We evaluated TapID in a series of userstudies on event-detection accuracy (F1 = 0.997) and hand-agnostic finger-identification accuracy (within-user: F1 = 0.93; across users: F1 = 0.91 after 10 refinement taps and F1 = 0.87 without refinement) in a seated table scenario. We conclude with a series of applications that complement hand tracking with touch input and that are uniquely enabled by TapID, including UI control, rapid keyboard typing and piano playing, as well as surface gestures.

papers.title: Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
papers.abstract: Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated six models from two vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for five of six models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 3.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for five models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, three models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin, but no model reached the pre-set 30% limits of agreement. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model (4.2 points) and changed the others by less than 1 point. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.

papers.title: Beyond Behavioral Accuracy: Evaluating Individual-Level Fidelity in LLM Investor Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as user simulators, but can they faithfully reproduce an individual's behavior and decision logic over time? We investigate this question in a longitudinal paper-trading study with 80 participants. Using rolling next-day predictions, we evaluate trading activity, buy-sell structure, asset selection, and portfolio outcomes, complemented by controlled input ablations and participant-rated explanation alignment. No evaluated LLM reliably outperforms a simple recent-activity persistence baseline for predicting trade occurrence, while buy-sell structure and asset selection remain difficult to reproduce. Similar activity-level performance can also yield substantially different portfolio trajectories. Ablations show that activity predictions depend primarily on recent trades, whereas asset choices are sensitive to multiple evidence sources. Participants rate explanations as more aligned with their recurring strategies than with their decision-specific rationales. These findings reveal a gap between coarse behavioral agreement and individual-level fidelity, motivating separate evaluation of behavioral accuracy, explanation alignment, and evidence dependence in personalized user simulation.

papers.title: Promptile: Recovering and Reusing Prompting Strategies from LLM Interaction Histories
papers.abstract: As people use large language models (LLMs) over time, they develop their own ways of prompting to achieve desired results. These useful experiences often remain scattered and unorganized across conversations. Yet existing personalization approaches primarily capture user preferences or explicitly defined workflows. Through a formative study, we found that users develop prompting strategies that range from implicit instructions to explicit templates from these experiences. We further find that interaction behaviors provide evidence for these strategies, which can be decomposed and recombined for reuse across tasks. Building on these findings, we present Promptile, a framework that identifies and validates users' prompting strategies from interaction histories. Promptile organizes these strategies into reusable components that can be retrieved, combined, and adapted to users' current tasks. Our evaluation shows that Promptile accurately recovers and reuses these strategies, better aligning model outputs with users' expectations while reducing repetitive prompting effort.

papers.title: Comparing Experiences of Speech-Driven Game Modification in Solo Play, Paired Play, and Paired Watching Using the Fighting Game PATCH FIGHTER
papers.abstract: Players often have ideas about a game while playing it, but turning them into changes usually means stepping out of play to edit it. We built PATCH FIGHTER, a two-player fighting game defined by 91 types of adjustable parameters. A large language model (LLM) reads players' conversations during play and rewrites these parameters between games, so players can change the game just by talking. We conducted a within-subjects experiment with 27 pairs (54 participants) comparing three conditions, solo play, paired play, and paired watching. Participants rated enjoyment after each game and answered a questionnaire on speech and changes after each condition. Paired play was the most enjoyable condition. In paired play, participants also felt more able to say what they thought about the game than in solo play. In interviews, participants valued talking with the partner and checking changes through their own play. Paired watching was less preferred because they could not try the changes themselves. As our design cannot separate the enjoyment of editing from that of play, we outline a design that measures them separately and the evaluation of the resulting games as future work.

papers.title: Exploring Visual Access and Proactive AI Tutoring for Handwritten Mathematics
papers.abstract: Handwritten work captures mathematical reasoning that learners may not express in typed or voice-dictated messages. We built a multimodal AI tutoring platform in which a phone camera gives the tutor a live view of learners' work on paper. In a randomized online study, 117 adults solved calculus problems with Text-Reactive, Visual-Reactive, or Visual-Proactive assistance. Analysis of 2,140 tutor messages showed that visual access shifted assistance toward checking ongoing work, while proactivity enhanced error identification and directive hints. Learners valued feedback grounded in their writing; those who received proactive help rated it as supportive, and about a third wanted it more often. These findings inform when tutors should intervene and what they should address. We release the platform, prompts, and instruments, together with 255,984 timestamped images of handwritten work linked to tutoring conversations, intervention decisions, and learning outcomes, to support multimodal tutoring systems that preserve the affordances of handwritten work while providing adaptive feedback.

papers.title: From Tasks to Turns: Measuring Human Labor Contributions in Human-Agent Joint Production
papers.abstract: In agent workflows, a brief human instruction can alter subsequent search, reasoning, and tool execution, yet final task outcomes rarely reveal the contribution of an individual instruction to human-agent joint production. We propose a Human Turn-level framework for measuring human contributions, using task quality and token usage to characterize the collaborative production outcomes associated with each human instruction. We compare continuations from adjacent checkpoints under matched models, budgets, and termination conditions, and assess stability through repeated measurements. Across four archived and simulated interaction settings, we conduct 29,124 comparisons between predicted and observed directions of quality and computational change at both Human Turn and session levels. On HumanBench, we obtain 506 valid comparisons across 85 real-user scenarios. Results show that quality and computational changes associated with human guidance depend on task conditions. Expert-style and ordinary-style guidance differ in information provision, correction, and repetition. Even when task quality after continuation is identical, remaining computational demands can differ substantially across checkpoints. Our framework advances the measurement of human labor contributions from tasks and sessions to individual turns, providing a repeatable, fine-grained foundation for studying human contributions and their allocation in human-agent joint production.

papers.title: Remote Expert Evaluation of Tabletop Avatar Gaze Control in Asymmetric Multi-Scale MR--VR Collaboration
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an integrated setup for a multi-scale asymmetric collaboration scenario in the context of a remote-expert use case, focusing on the expert side. In this system, the remote expert (with an exocentric view in Mixed Reality (MR)) uses a Tangible User Interface (TUI) to precisely position and rotate their avatar within a scaled tabletop World-in-Miniature (WIM). Inside the WIM, the expert's avatar and the operator share the same scale and egocentric view, while the expert retains a global tabletop overview of the plant to support collaboration. Interviews with industry experts during the participatory design phase revealed the need for an egocentric view inside the plant on the remote-expert side to enable full collaboration. We designed and studied three interaction-visualisation combinations to integrate and control the expert avatar's gaze: VR (fully immersive with direct head control), Head (floating screen with direct head control), and Touch (on-avatar screen with touchpad control). We evaluated these methods with 29 participants across two fault-detection tasks: Same Machine, where both collaborators inspect the same machine, and Twin Machine, where they inspect identical machines in separate locations. The VR condition, which combines immersion, direct head control, and a full-scale view, yielded the strongest overall performance and user experience, while the tabletop avatar setup was well received for collaboration. Our findings inform the design of gaze-control techniques for asymmetric MR-VR collaboration and reveal challenges and opportunities for future work.

papers.title: SplatXR: A Toolkit for Multi-Layered Extended Reality via On-Headset 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting, 3D foundation models, and video-passthrough mixed reality offer unprecedented fidelity for capturing and blending physical and virtual worlds. However, established XR methods rely on polygon-based pipelines that treat physical and digital environments as separate domains, making seamless integration across recent novel representations difficult. Because splats lack explicit surface geometry, they impede standard graphics techniques necessary for cross-reality interactions, such as shadow or collision handling. Furthermore, while 3D foundation models can reconstruct physical objects on-the-fly into digital splats, current XR systems fall short of leveraging this capability for user experiences that transition seamlessly between physicality and virtuality. To address this, we organize XR as a multi-layered reality of interacting primitives, letting pixels and objects move across physical and digital boundaries. We contribute SplatXR, a Unity toolkit that operationalizes this structure as building blocks for interactive, immersive apps leveraging 3D Gaussian splatting: a standalone renderer, splat-to-mesh reconstruction, splat physics, splat blending, and offloaded splat object reconstruction via on-headset capture. SplatXR unites vision and graphics techniques to make splat-based XR development broadly available, and we validate it through demonstrative applications and a small developer study.

papers.title: Bringing physics-based controller policies to virtual reality
papers.abstract: Nowadays, it is easy to set up any element of a VR experience so users can interact with it physically, except for interactive VR characters. Can we extend this to animated VR characters? In this work, we studied whether physics-based character animation (PBCA) controllers can produce high-quality movement in VR-compatible environments (Unity3D, WebXR). We evaluated the quality of the results, as well as the losses at each stage of the processing pipeline: data ingest, training and inference. For data ingest, we computed accuracy metrics related to the retargeting method used. For training, we computed accuracy metrics related to different training policies and different training environments. We developed new JAX implementations of state-of-the-art PBCA controllers (DeepMimic, AMP and ADD) which can be trained in MuJoCo-MJX in minutes, 50 times faster than in a traditional CPU-based training environment. The benefit of these particular implementations is that the resulting control policies can be readily transferred to Unity3D and support cross-platform compilation, including Android, something critical for use in VR production. For inference, we tested these controller policies in Unity3D and WebXR. Our results suggest that DeepMimic and ADD trained in MuJoCo-MJX generate controller policies with better animation fidelity than other methods. To simplify the comparison between controller policies, and different reference animations, we implemented an animation fidelity index (afi). Its results are analogous to other more common metrics, but afi is more intuitive to interpret and thus simplifies the comparison of training methods across the successive stages of the processing pipeline.

papers.title: Context-Aware Topological Distillation Graph Network for Asymmetric EEG-Eye Movement Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: EEG-eye movement emotion recognition can support mental-health monitoring and adaptive interfaces, but most fusion models treat the two signals as parallel features, classify each window alone and degrade when eye data are lost. We propose the Context-Aware Topological Distillation Graph Network (CTD-GNet), in which EEG features form the nodes of an electrode graph, and eye movements and preceding windows modulate its edges, nodes and readout, the edges through electrode-specific prompts. Bidirectional distillation of the graph, node relations and predictions couples this multimodal teacher with a single-window EEG student, improving the teacher and aligning the two graphs 35-fold. In leave-one-subject-out tests on SEED and SEED-IV against 17 baselines, CTD-GNet has the highest mean accuracy, 84.91% and 76.17%, significantly above 9 and 6 of 13 eye-based baselines after Holm correction, the smallest cross-subject spread among multimodal models and the highest worst-subject accuracy. It is the most accurate model at every rate of missing eye data on SEED-IV, keeps 66.1% on SEED without eye data, more than any EEG-only model, and stays 9.3 and 11.9 points above all single-window fusion models under eye-movement noise of one standard deviation. On film clips unseen in training, it leads on SEED with 77.1%.

papers.title: Cling: Supporting Cross-Page Coordination with Human-Directed, In-Situ, and Small-Step Automation
papers.abstract: Web-based information work spans independently developed pages, with goals and coordination needs often emerging through browsing. Manual coordination requires repeated low-level actions, yet explicitly specifying operations for automation can interrupt engagement with information that shapes users' next steps. Our approach constructs reusable, schema-based page representations and identifies coordination actions through correspondences across schemas. We instantiate this approach in Cling, which surfaces coordination opportunities in situ for users to select, configure, and execute incrementally while directing the broader task. A technical evaluation demonstrates accurate identification of useful opportunities across diverse domains. A 12-participant study found that Cling reduced task durations by more than half compared with both manual interaction and an end-to-end AI agent, while requiring 61% fewer clicks and 80% fewer tab switches than manual interaction. Its small-step automation supported control and verification as actions unfolded, while accommodating intent as it emerged and evolved through information encountered on the page.

papers.title: When Care Expands and Control Declines: Understanding Digital Privacy in End-of-Life Care
papers.abstract: Terminally ill patients generate extensive digital health data through hospital portals, physiological monitoring devices, consumer health applications, and end-of-life care platforms. Yet their ability to control this data is systematically undermined by the structural conditions of terminal care. Through semi-structured in-depth interviews with 21 terminally ill patients, 11 family caregivers, and 8 physicians recruited from tertiary hospitals, this study examines the digital privacy circumstances and subjective attitudes of patients in end-of-life contexts. Thematic analysis reveals five structural dimensions of digital privacy challenge: continuous bodily digitization without meaningful informed consent; cognitive decline driving involuntary proxy control of accounts; inferential data generation exceeding patients' epistemic boundaries; dissolution of individual privacy boundaries amid relational network restructuring; and the absence of institutional governance over post-mortem data. Patient privacy attitudes span three profiles: fundamental absence of privacy awareness, sustained active management under severe tool constraints, and perception of problems followed by resigned abandonment. Interviews with caregivers and physicians reveal benevolent substitution in the name of care needs, expansion of access beyond the initial task, and unresolved boundaries under absent institutional guidance. These findings reveal a compounding privacy vulnerability unique to end-of-life contexts and call for privacy-by-design principles, granular permission mechanisms, and institutional governance frameworks tailored to the needs of dying patients.

papers.title: When Better Opportunities Backfire: Service Worker Responses to Parallel AI Deployment in Customer Acquisition
papers.abstract: As AI voice agents get deployed in high-volume contact centers, firms can route low-intent leads to AI and allocate high-intent leads to human workers. Drawing on sequential search theory, we posit that AI-induced task allocation reshapes work, enriching opportunities facing human workers but also raising their reservation value for continuing with the lead in hand, making them less willing to persist. We study the effects of an AI voice-agent deployment at a Chinese online health-insurance brokerage using more than a half million customer outreach records surrounding the rollout. Adopting a regression-discontinuity-in-time design, we trace how worker behavior changes across the workday. Results show that the enrichment of human-facing opportunities concentrates early in the workday, raising the probability that a call is a high-intent lead by about 23 percentage points on the first three calls and fading to zero later. However, customer acquisition by human workers declines precisely where the enrichment is greatest, falling about 5 percentage points on the first three calls and flattening over the day. Consistent with the theorized reservation value mechanism, workers reallocate their earliest leads about 8 percentage points more often and persist less with them, shortening those calls by about 13%. A calibrated decomposition analysis further shows that the modest gain from improved lead ordering is outweighed by a much larger negative behavioral response. By reshaping the quality and within-workday distribution of opportunities, parallel AI deployment alters how workers pursue tasks, highlighting opportunity distribution as an important service operations state variable beyond workload and congestion.

papers.title: Voice-Based AI Feedback in Higher Education: A Field Study on Quality and Actionability
papers.abstract: Student feedback is a critical input for continuous improvement in higher education, yet traditional end-of-semester written surveys suffer from low response rates, superficial answers, satisficing, and limited actionability. Voice-based conversational AI agents can conduct structured interviews at scale, asking open-ended questions and probing follow-ups, and may capture richer qualitative feedback than written instruments. This research proposal asks what characteristics, depth, and strategic value feedback collected through voice-based conversational AI agents has in higher education, and whether such agents elicit detailed, honest, and actionable feedback that can support instructional improvement and institutional learning. Drawing on survey-mode-effects research, the Computers As Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, and dynamic capabilities theory, we develop three hypotheses on elaboration, social presence and disclosure, and actionability. A completed technical pilot at the Technical University of Munich established the feasibility of telephone-based AI interviews; the main field study is planned for the "Advanced Leadership Communication" course at MIT Sloan with approximately 60 students, using a convergent mixed-methods design and a four-dimensional coding framework for actionability (specificity, thematic richness, constructive orientation, contextual depth). The study extends CASA theory to evaluative educational settings, characterizes voice-based AI as a distinct feedback modality, and links micro-level feedback quality to institutional sensing capabilities.

papers.title: AI-Mediated Employee Voice and Performance: Disentangling Informational and Affective Pathways
papers.abstract: Employee voice -- the discretionary expression of ideas, concerns, and suggestions intended to improve organizational functioning -- creates value inside firms, yet organizations increasingly replace or augment human-led listening with AI-enabled systems that collect, analyze, and route employee input at scale. Whether algorithmic listening replicates the value-creation mechanisms of human voice, and whether it alters the pathways through which voice translates into performance, remains an open question. This research proposal theorizes that traditional voice bundles two distinct functions, knowledge extraction and relational signaling, and that AI mediation may decouple them: strengthening the informational pathway (implemented improvement measures) while weakening the affective pathway (the experience of being heard). We propose a randomized field intervention at a global strategy consulting firm, covering approximately 2,000 client-facing consultants, that varies the form of listening across three conditions -- no structured voice, human-led survey-based voice, and AI-enabled conversational voice -- and links weekly team survey data to longitudinal performance ratings. A dual-mediation model is tested in which voice affects performance through (1) implemented process improvements and (2) affective well-being. The study extends voice theory to knowledge-intensive professional services, disentangles the micro-mechanisms of voice, and provides causal evidence on whether AI can serve as an effective listener.

papers.title: When Interpretations Persist: Downstream Influence in Gaze-Aware Assistants
papers.abstract: AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.

papers.title: Simulating Infant Senses with Age-Tuned Networks
papers.abstract: What a newborn sees, hears and feels, and how this changes month by month, has been measured sense by sense, with different methods and in different units. We bring these measurements together for the first two years of life and ask whether small neural networks tuned to a given age can turn them into a quick, inspectable simulation of sensory perception. Each sense's immaturity is written as a fixed, age-indexed filter on the input, and a small prediction network learns behind it over the first year. The filters alone reproduce the order in which the senses mature, by construction. The networks add what filters cannot: in vision they extract far less than their input allows at early stages (at the newborn stage a toy's position cannot be read out, $R^2 = 0.00$, against 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in; in hearing they track what their input allows. The same filters drive the Baby Senses Lab, a free website that shows a user's own images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might sense them. It is a research and teaching tool, not a diagnostic test.

papers.title: UnexpectedParrots: Iterating Behavioral Experiment Design with In-Silico Simulations
papers.abstract: Running behavioral experiments is expensive, slow, and prone to design flaws, often detectable after collecting data. We introduce UnexpectedParrots to iteratively refine behavioral study designs before a researcher recruits costly human participants.
